story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Mark. Companies are really pushing cloud agents, but I found myself wanting to run agents on my Mac off-hours on my existing Claude/Codex subs.

I'd hit my usage limit coding with Fable, but not my limit on other models for tasks like marketing, research and content creation. So I built an orchestrator that organizes my agents into departments (or ships) where they have overriding goals/milestones and a "captain" agent can spawn other agents working in that department.

I think this structure works better than individual agent workers in an office. (Mundler Difflin)

The user can prompt the agent dispatcher for one-off or recurring tasks, which can be controlled from a Slack or a Telegram bot. Since Overboard has context about all your local projects it knows where it should spawn an agent. You can also talk to department heads or the main agent to see what human blockers are stalling projects, or give new direction for a department. Would love to hear feedback about the project. It's not open-source but there is a 14 day trial so anyone can test if it's useful before buying a license. (one-time $49)

story_text.value:
Upfront caveat: it's English only! but I'm personally still just amazed that 34MB (fine-tuned BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 ) can fit so much knowledge that it's possible to have an iPhone 15 running these classifications entirely client-side on arbitrary english text in 10-30ms.

The game is a little trivial but thought it was a cool showcase, you type messages to the guard and they get classified as either friendly, bribe, threats, etc.

I've been playing a lot with Jev use-cases since it came out and then learned about fine-tuning my own models.

The way I went about it was just using Jev first via a proxy to record my calls and store them as my own training data to make running training easier. I built a whole oss platform around doing that with models (of various sizes) https://github.com/doppsh/dopp.

Would love to hear any feedback / discuss more on either that whole training process or the game itself.

Also I did get a ton of help from Opus doing all this, so some things might be a little rough around some edges but plenty of human time has been put in too. Very welcoming of any feedback/criticism

I created an open source alternative to tools like Instantly or Smartlead, which charge huge amounts of money per lead for basic cold email campaign management.

The emails are sent from your inbox, and you get open rates and analytics for your campaign.

It also comes with an MCP server, so you can manage the whole campaign from Claude or Codex.

It also has multi email option, so you can spread the senders through various emails as you like, and many other things like classification of replies or automatic draft reply generation.

If you like the project, you can sign up and use the hosted version and if you star the Github project it would help it grow!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Ciao to solve problems I was experiencing:

1. Connecting to a new host should be as seamless as possible. I SSH a lot nowadays, and I find the key sharing across devices cumbersome.

2. I get annoyed by setting up insert-your-favorite VPN on new machines. They're all great. I don't want to think about them.

3. There's a lot of harnesses: Claude Code and Codex now have decent mobile push notifications but what about Pi or xyz-shiny-new harness? The harness is another tool that should be abstracted out.

4. I want a single application that has the big picture of all of my agents. Tmux and Herdr are great but they don't have an overview of all my connected machines' agents.

---

With Ciao you curl|sh the daemon --> run ciao pair --> point your phone's camera at the QR code --> and you're connected. It uses iroh for accountless and E2EE connection. There's an optional relay server for APNS which too is E2EE.

One of my favorite aspects of agentic-engineering is being able to just have a lot of fun with programming. Among many features, I built a visually pleasing toggle between terminal-mode and native-chat-mode. If you install Ciao, come back here and tell me what you think.

---

Full transparency: this is a repost from yesterday, it was a massive day in AI.

story_text.value:
Light it up with Hypercolor, a new RGB lighting orchestration platform for all platforms and all devices. Effects are web pages (or glsl), rendered by an internal browser GPU accelerated all the way to the pixels. It's pure rust from the Servo renderer to the WASM UI.

Comes with 40+ effects, supports ambilight, display faces, system monitoring, screen casting, and audio. Device support is pretty good but it's early and this is where we need the most help! You can find the full support matrix on the site, and there is also an OpenRGB bridge as a fallback. There's support for a few unique devices too like the Ableton Push 2 and ROLI Blocks. My favorite thing about this engine is the ability to create multiple effect zones and manage them independently! My whole house runs on it now. It's Apache licensed, and a cloud service is coming with remote and smart home support. A Home Assistant integration is already available.

The best way to set up Hypercolor is to just have an agent do it for you using the bundled skill. Just describe your setup, case type, hardware, etc, and it will find all the specs and configure it for you. Or just do it the good old-fashioned way in Studio!

Please check it out and file and issue if you're looking for device support. I can only build drivers for devices I have access too, please open PRs if you're able to contribute! Agents can reverse engineer your hardware and build a driver easily, if you want to go that route (the repo is designed for agents). We have a full TypeScript effects SDK for easy effect creation too, and support existing Lightscript based html effects out of the box.

I've had a lot of fun building this and I hope you enjoy it!

story_text.value:
I'm a fan of Techmeme, which clusters tech news by topic, so I decided to do the same with edtech and help me keep up with edtech. But it helped only a little. Unlike in tech, where daily news is usually heavily clusterable because people comment on daily trending topics like apple's latest launch etc., in edtech, we don't really have these trending topics often, but we do have these persistent ongoing beats like AI in education or Edtech policy etc. So I decided to leverage the help of the newly released Jev model (a model that's super fast and cheap and works great with categorization tasks) to help categorize these items into different topics and tags, which seems to work really great so far (and has kept the cost low).

In terms of implementation, it's basically a pipeline that processes a list of sources consisting of trade media and indie newsletters and blogs with RSS feeds, and tags them with Jev using a hierarchy of topics related to edtech. Users can follow and pin individual topics, like "higher ed", "Europe" etc., so we don't need any persistent profiles for personalization; preferences live in the browser. Articles are clustered using cloudflare's vector store, and related articles are also recommended with that.

I have no doubt this will work even better with tech news, but there are plenty of alternatives out there, so I'm not going to indulge myself further. My takeaway is that Jev for content tagging is great so far. And edtech is kinda fun to keep up with.

The project is called EdFountain at https://edfountain.com

The goal is to create the water fountain for edtech.

For those who like to follow edtech, maybe it's useful to you as well. Feel free to drop a coin and make a wish on the /about page if you have other source recommendations. :D

story_text.value:
I’m Ruggiero, a CS student working on a research project about humanComputer interaction and AI.

I built QUIET because I’ve been thinking about a problem with current AI interfaces: they usually either wait for an explicit prompt, or try to take over a task.

I wanted to explore a different relationship between humans and AI: an assistant that can understand when to stay out of the way, when to point something out, when to teach, and when to act. I’ve built a small interactive demo of this idea. It’s obviously still very early, and I want to understand whether the interaction itself makes sense before trying to build the actual AI system behind it.

The prototype is intentionally not AI-powered yet.

The four examples are scripted so I can test the interaction itself before spending time building the underlying AI system.

The idea is that the assistant can choose different levels/forms of intervention:

* stay silent * point at something * explain / teach * do the task

The important question for me isn’t whether an AI can perform these actions. Current systems can already do many of them.

I’m trying to understand whether an assistant that decides when and how much to intervene is actually useful.

I’d particularly like feedback on:

* Did the interventions feel helpful or annoying? * Would you want an assistant to behave this way? * When would you prefer it to teach you rather than do something for you? * Does this interaction model make sense even without the AI being there yet?

I started working on this because I feel there is an increasing gap between what computers/AI are capable of and what users actually understand and can make use of. At the same time, AI systems are becoming increasingly capable of explaining and performing tasks for us.

I’m interested in whether the interface itself should evolve to bridge that gap.

Demo: https://quiet-hci.pages.dev

I’d really appreciate any criticism, especially if you think the interaction model doesn’t make sense.

The demo suit best the desktop screens on phones Im working on a totally different but also similar idea of interaction, and since this is a simulation of the desktop tool it should work best on it , Thank You <3

story_text.value:
Hi folks,

I've been lurking here for a while, and after almost two months of building, I finally dared to share what I've been working on.

It's called Kyno (pronounced KAI-no). It's what I call a coherence control plane: it treats direction as a first-class primitive, expressed as a constitution with a mission and principles that agents can pull at each step of a workflow.

The goal is to enable principled decision-making, bottom-up agency, and self-governance in agents.

Kyno doesn't rely on LLMs. It's a lightweight system that provides centralized, versioned direction so agents can exercise judgment while staying aligned with the mission. It can work independently or complement AI governance tools, pairing boundaries with principles to support greater autonomy over time.

It's free to use and open-core. If you're interested, please take a look, I'd love some feedback.

Thank you all!

https://cizambra.github.io/kyno/

story_text.value:
This is Katriel, the architect of the tool APIaxess.

I have been API pentesting for a good time now, and starting with API pentesting was a bit of a rough patch. Specially the setting up and having to know the intricacies of proxies, networking and other stuff. Then once i got through it, the next rough patch was the apk pentesting, where getting the traffic of any apk was more of a task then the pentesting itself. So i started by writing scripts that automates the process and then made sure that any rooted adb just automatically started sending traffic to the burpsuite setup, and then that helped a lot. Then i just thought that this issue needs to be resolved in a more open manner, since its a very known pain point. So i built a GUI around it, made sure that it can handle everything that a normal api traffic tool can and then thought of releasing it, for people to test it out. Before the inital release, i have myself battle tested this tool, in multiple ways, while also sharing it with other professionals in my industry who constantly use Burp/Caido/HTTPToolkit or other similar tools. I know that the tool needs more features and more refinements, but thought of making it public so that i can get to know about the issues much sooner.

Do check out the Github and leave a star if it helped you out, and do share it with your colleagues so that they could also waste less time setting it up and more time doing the work that they like. github.com/KatrielMoses/apiaxess

story_text.value:
Hey HN! Yolanda and Spencer here - wanted to share a token compression tool that we’ve built for ourselves to save 30% costs on codex!

After maxing out sub and burning $700/day per person on api, we fine tuned a compression model to trim codex's tool call output to reduce input token + cache. It cut down tokens by 29.6% and now I just leave it on by default in Codex.

To avoid messing up w/ cache, we use proxy + fine tuned qwen model trained on preserving agent trajectory to remove tool call results before they go back to the model, leaving kv cache untouched.

The cli is free for everyone to use (https://github.com/spenmcke/compress). Just lmk ur feedback and hacks to shave even more costs on astra! If you want to integrate it into your product to offer the best models at low cost, I can set you up with an sdk and api keys

PS: It’s built for coding agents, not conversational agents. I optimized it for file retrieval accuracy, trajectory preservation, and quality to get up to 30% cost reduction depending on how context-heavy the task is.

On security and privacy side, it's a proxy wrapping your local codex and ZDR so it doesn't retain any queries. It’s on by default in codex and when you don’t want compression, you can use `codex --uncompress` to disable it.

Give it a try: code is in https://github.com/spenmcke/compress

You can install the cli using

`curl -fsSL https://install.everestagi.com/install.sh | sh && source ~/.config/everest/shell.sh`

Love to hear any feedback and learn your hacky ways to save token costs too!

To avoid messing up w/ cache, we use proxy + fine tuned qwen model trained on preserving agent trajectory to remove tool call results before they go back to the model, leaving kv cache untouched.

The cli is free for everyone to use (https://github.com/spenmcke/compress). Just lmk ur feedback and hacks to shave even more costs on astra! If you want to integrate it into your product to offer the best models at low cost, I can set you up with an sdk and api keys

PS: It’s built for coding agents, not conversational agents. I optimized it for file retrieval accuracy, trajectory preservation, and quality to get up to 30% cost reduction depending on how context-heavy the task is.

On security and privacy side, it's a proxy wrapping your local codex and ZDR so it doesn't retain any queries. It’s on by default in codex and when you don’t want compression, you can use `codex --uncompress` to disable it.

Give it a try: code is in https://github.com/spenmcke/compress

You can install the cli using

`curl -fsSL https://install.everestagi.com/install.sh | sh && source ~/.config/everest/shell.sh`

Love to hear any feedback and learn your hacky ways to save token costs too!

ios/android supported!

story_text.value: I've been working on a implicit text to cad system (scratchcad) that outputs STL. This is all built around fidget, a really cool experimental implicit engine by Matt Keeter. Scratchcad adds a rust http API on top of fidget and provides an mcp for any agent to interact with the API, so that it can script in Rhai, verify it's scripts and create STLs. My whole system is under Apache 2 so that anyone can build with it. It's still super early but I excited to see where this goes and what you all model or build on top of scratchcad.

story_text.value:
A few months ago we started building a model router for coding agents because we thought we could outperform any single model with an ensemble approach. Recently we’ve achieved that milestone and I want to talk about how we did it.

First of all, a quick explanation: the Weave Router (https://github.com/weave-os/router) plugs into any coding agent (e.g. Claude Code or Codex) and intelligently switches between LLMs. So, for example, Astra handles tricky debugging or complex system design tasks, and Deepseek v4 Flash handles simple frontend updates.

What we’re announcing today is our new routing model, which we’re calling Weave Router 2.0. We benchmarked 2.0 against GPT-6 Astra on Terminal Bench 4.0 and SWE Atlas. On both benchmarks, the router had equivalent pass rates. On Terminal Bench, the router hit 52% of Astra’s cost, and completed tasks 2.2x faster. On SWE Atlas, the router cost 54% as much as Astra and ran 2.5x faster. (Full results on our website at https://weaveos.com/router!)

It turns out training a model to route effectively - taking into consideration model capabilities, costs, cache awareness, and more - is a really hard problem! I want to talk about three ways we were able to improve so much over the last few months: 1) a new architecture, 2) larger training data set size, and 3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation.

1) a new architecture. Our initial approach used an RL model without many priors. While RL is still an important part of the story, the cost of fully exploring the space of routing decisions is very high, so we’ve taken some shortcuts that have significantly improved performance. In particular: we trained a hidden Markov model to trace the session state, then a classifier maps the session to one of a few buckets of similar models. This significantly shrinks the space to explore, by throwing out most models that could not reasonably serve the given session. This rearchitecture was the single biggest performance unlock!

Consider how large the search space for the routing problem is. Take a typical coding agent session, with ~100 agent turns (i.e. 100 LLM API calls). Technically there are 100 chances to select a model. If we assume a roster of ~10 models (of course there are lots more but we can remove any that are Pareto dominated), then there are 10^100 possible paths through that session. We simply cannot explore all of them! So that's why clever tricks to shrink this space are so important.

2) larger training data set size (much less technically interesting but still an important part of the story). By using frontier LLMs to help us label a larger and more diverse set of coding agent sessions, we were able to bootstrap the two models discussed in 1) to a better state, while also providing even richer reward signals for RL.

3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation. One of the hardest parts of routing well (if you care about saving money) is using the model caches intelligently. We built a subsystem that can calculate the expected value of switching models (and thus paying a high one-time cost to fill up a different cache) much more accurately, helping us avoid costly and unnecessary switches in more cases, while still switching when the benefit outweighs the cost. This is where most of our improvement on cost has come from.

We still have a lot of room to continue to improve (we won’t rest until we’re consistently beating Astra/Fable, not just tying!) but matching frontier model performance was a huge milestone for our routing model, and in my opinion validates our initial hypothesis that an ensemble of models can do better than any single model ever could.

Our router is open source (https://github.com/weave-os/router) so anyone can try it out. Or if you prefer you can use our hosted version (https://weaveos.com/router).
